doc.title: Roy Haynes — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Not wanting to relive the past in an interview
summary: Haynes says going back over difficult times irritates him once he has dealt with them.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: Let’s go back to ’54, your trip to Europe.
Did we want to ex- . . . no. Okay.

No, because then you started getting into laying out and you made me think – you see, that’s what I mean about – you start re-living certain things over again as you talk about them. Then sometimes it’s something that you don’t want to re-live over again. You know what I mean? So that’s why I said, “Please.” It’s not – we went back into . . .
You’ve got the up and downs.

Yeah, but when you have to deal with it in life, you deal with it, you cope with it. But then after that, if you finished cope with it and think that you’ve overcome it or you’re through with that obstacle, whatever it is, if it’s not an obstacle, or whatever it is. Like in school, when there was a test, I couldn’t wait to finish that … …, regardless if I thought I did it good or not. So now we say, “It’s life,” true, it’s life, but it’s behind you, and when you keep bringing it back – it’s like something in your stomach that’s irritating, you can bring it back in here, aaaaaaaaah, here it comes again. You understand what I’m trying to say?
